strengths: Compelling theoretical unification: The paper provides an elegant reverse inferential perspective on flow matching without target samples, framing the training target as posterior mean estimation.

Principled variance reduction via Stein operators: The use of Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates for vector-valued posterior means is mathematically rigorous, and the closed-form derivation of the asymptotic variance-minimizing coefficients (Propositions 4 and 5) is well-grounded.

Unifying perspective on existing literature: The manuscript clearly demonstrates in Theorem 2 and Appendix B that existing noise-expectation methods (e.g., QNE, SDAC) and gradient-expectation methods (e.g., iDEM, DQS) correspond to specific choices (\eta = 0 and \eta = 1) within the proposed control variate family.
Clarity and presentation: The mathematical exposition is well-structured, easy to follow, and supported by detailed appendices extending the concepts to reverse score matching.
weaknesses: Limited empirical evaluation and reporting: The experimental section spans less than one page with eight DMC environments shown only in small plots (Figure 1). There is no tabular summary of final scores, no aggregate statistical metrics (such as interquartile mean or performance profiles recommended in modern RL benchmarks), and no evaluation on more challenging or multi-modal benchmarks.

Lack of critical ablation studies: While the theory emphasizes that the optimal control variate combines Q-values and Q-gradients to achieve minimal variance, there is no empirical ablation isolating the gain from the control variate (e.g., comparing RFM with optimal \Lambda^* directly against RFM with \eta = 0 and \eta = 1 on the exact same flow backbone). It remains unclear how much of the performance advantage comes from the flow architecture versus the variance reduction.

Missing analysis of computational overhead: Estimating the posterior mean with the optimal control variate requires computing both Q-evaluations and Q-gradients for N samples per update, as well as computing the empirical moments for \Lambda^*. The manuscript lacks a discussion or measurement of wall-clock training time and sample efficiency trade-offs compared to diffusion baselines.

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: The paper does not explore sensitivity to critical parameters, such as the number of importance samples N, proposal distributions \hat{p}_t, or the temperature parameter \lambda.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical unification: The paper frames training diffusion/flow policies under unnormalized target densities from a reverse inferential perspective, successfully connecting the conditional flow matching formulation to posterior mean estimation.

Novel use of Langevin Stein control variates: By introducing matrix-valued Langevin Stein operators, the authors derive a flexible class of zero-mean control variates for self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), including closed-form variance-minimizing coefficients (Propositions 4 and 5).

Conceptual clarity across prior literature: The framework unifies previously disconnected families of methods—specifically noise-expectation approaches (e.g., QNE, RSM, corresponding to $\eta=0$) and gradient-expectation approaches (e.g., iDEM, DQS, corresponding to $\eta=1$)—showing them to be special cases of a single control-variate formulation.
Strong empirical performance: Across eight continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite, RFM demonstrates consistent learning and superior stability compared to SAC, QSM, QNE, and DQS.
Clear mathematical presentation and well-organized exposition.
weaknesses: Lack of targeted ablation studies: The empirical gains could stem either from the flow matching formulation (ODE integration) or from the optimal control variate coefficients $\Lambda^*$. An ablation comparing RFM against RFM with $\eta=0$ (pure noise expectation) and $\eta=1$ (pure gradient expectation) on the exact same flow backbone is necessary to isolate the effect of variance reduction.

No empirical variance quantification: While the theoretical reduction of asymptotic variance is proven, the paper does not empirically report the sample variance of the posterior mean estimator $\hat{\mu}$ across different values of $\Lambda$ or sample size $N$ during training.

Computational overhead is not analyzed: Estimating $\Lambda^*$ and evaluating the control variate requires evaluating Q-function gradients $\nabla_a Q(s, a)$ across all $N$ importance samples per training step. A comparison of wall-clock time and memory overhead against baselines like QNE (which only requires scalar Q evaluations) should be provided.

strengths: Principled Theoretical Unification: The paper establishes a rigorous and elegant theoretical framework (Reverse Flow Matching) that unites two previously disparate families of algorithms for Boltzmann distribution targeting in diffusion/flow RL—namely the noise-expectation family (e.g., QNE, SDAC) and the gradient-expectation family (e.g., iDEM, DQS)—showing that they correspond to specific parameterizations (eta=0 and eta=1) of Langevin Stein control variates.

Variance Reduction Formulation: By formulating the training target as a posterior mean estimation problem and deriving optimal variance-minimizing control variates via generalized Langevin Stein operators (Propositions 4 and 5), the work directly addresses the high variance inherent in self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) for energy-based policy learning.

Generality Across Frameworks: The formulation seamlessly accommodates general linear interpolations, encompassing both flow matching and standard diffusion noise schedules (variance-preserving and variance-exploding), and applies to velocity, data, noise, and score parameterizations.
Clear Presentation: The mathematical derivations are clean, well-organized, and straightforward to follow from the background up to the practical RL algorithm.
weaknesses: Lack of Component-Level Ablations: In the empirical section, RFM (which uses flow matching and optimal control variates) is compared against baseline algorithms that differ in multiple confounding ways (e.g., diffusion vs. flow backbone, schedule choices, and estimator form). An isolated ablation study within the exact same flow model comparing the optimal control variate against eta=0 (pure noise expectation) and eta=1 (pure gradient expectation) is missing, making it difficult to attribute empirical gains specifically to the Langevin Stein variance reduction versus the flow matching dynamics.

Limited Evaluation Diversity: The empirical evaluation is restricted to eight standard DeepMind Control Suite continuous control tasks. Demonstrating scalability on higher-dimensional or more challenging control benchmarks (e.g., Humanoid, Adroit hand manipulation, or Meta-World) would strengthen the practical significance of the method.

Computational Overhead and Sensitivity: The proposed SNIS estimator with control variates requires evaluating both Q-values and their action gradients over N samples per update. The paper does not provide empirical wall-clock time comparisons against standard methods or a sensitivity analysis regarding the number of samples N.

Unrealized Potential of Non-Gaussian Priors in Practice: Although the paper emphasizes that flow matching facilitates general source distributions beyond standard Gaussians, the online RL instantiation and experiments still rely exclusively on the standard Gaussian prior.

strengths: Compelling theoretical unification: The paper introduces Reverse Flow Matching (RFM) and provides a rigorous, principled view showing that the previously disjoint noise-expectation (e.g., QNE, RSM) and gradient-expectation (e.g., iDEM, DQS) families are specific instantiations (corresponding to $\eta=0$ and $\eta=1$) of posterior mean estimation with Langevin Stein control variates.

Principled variance reduction: By formulating the posterior mean estimation with matrix-valued Langevin Stein operators, the paper derives optimal closed-form coefficients that minimize the asymptotic variance of self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), directly combining Q-value and Q-gradient information.

Methodological completeness: The extension of flow matching to Boltzmann policies properly accounts for bounded action spaces via invertible transformations with the exact change-of-variables log-Jacobian correction, avoiding ad-hoc heuristic truncation.

Strong empirical performance and efficiency: RFM demonstrates superior performance and training stability across eight continuous-control environments from DeepMind Control Suite, achieving competitive or superior results with only 10 ODE integration steps compared to 20 or more steps required by diffusion baselines.

Clear presentation and thorough ablations: The manuscript is exceptionally well-structured and written. The theoretical proofs, sensitivity studies (over Monte Carlo samples $K$, action candidates $M$, and integration steps $N$), proposal distribution choices, and control variate ablations are comprehensive.
weaknesses: Evaluation domain complexity: The empirical evaluation is primarily conducted on standard DeepMind Control Suite environments with relatively low-to-moderate action dimensions. Demonstrating performance on more complex, high-dimensional control benchmarks (e.g., Humanoid, Isaac Gym/Orbit, or dexterous manipulation tasks) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Inference candidate selection heuristic: The policy execution relies on generating $M=32$ candidate actions and picking the one with the maximum Q-value. While this best-of-$M$ selection is common in recent literature (e.g., MaxEntDP, QVPO), isolating raw flow sampling performance without critic ranking across all environments would provide cleaner insight into the generative fidelity of the learned policy.

Computational overhead of critic evaluations: Estimating the posterior mean via SNIS with $K=100$ samples and evaluating Q-gradients requires non-trivial computational overhead per actor update, even though JAX vectorization keeps wall-clock time reasonable.

strengths: Compelling theoretical unification: The paper provides an elegant reverse inferential perspective on flow and diffusion policies targeting unnormalized Boltzmann distributions. Formulating the target as posterior mean estimation and using Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates elegantly unifies two previously separate paradigms (noise-expectation methods like QNE/RSM and gradient-expectation methods like iDEM/DQS) as special cases of a single general family.

Principled extension to flow policies: While prior Boltzmann-targeting works were strictly tied to diffusion formulations with specific noise schedules (VP or VE SDEs), this work successfully extends the paradigm to flow matching, allowing faster sampling at inference time (e.g., 10 ODE steps vs. 20-100 diffusion steps) without sacrificing sample quality.

Rigorous action bound handling: Rather than using heuristic bounding or ad-hoc Gaussian truncation that distorts probability paths, the paper introduces an unconstrained latent flow mapped via tanh, correctly accounting for the log-determinant Jacobian factor in the latent target density.

Thorough empirical evaluation and ablation study: The method is validated on a 2D two-moon toy benchmark and across eight DeepMind Control Suite continuous-control tasks. The authors provide thorough ablations comparing the adaptive control variate against the fixed cases (recovering noise-only and gradient-only estimators), varying proposal distributions, and analyzing hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Scope of RL benchmark domains: The continuous-control evaluation is restricted to standard DeepMind Control Suite tasks (e.g., Cartpole, Walker, Finger, Cheetah). While informative, these environments have relatively low action dimensions (typically $\le 6$). Evaluating on higher-dimensional or more contact-rich/multi-modal tasks (such as Humanoid, Shadow Hand / Adroit, or Meta-World) would more decisively demonstrate the scalability and multi-modality benefits of flow policies over Gaussian baselines like SAC.

Theoretical vs. practical alignment regarding the soft Q-function: The theoretical derivation in Section 3 relies on soft policy iteration where the policy targets $\exp(\frac{1}{\lambda} Q^\pi)$, yet in practice (Section 4.4 and Appendix G.2) the method trains a standard critic without the entropy regularization term (as computing flow log-likelihood requires expensive Hutchinson trace estimates or augmented ODE integration). While this is well-motivated empirically, the gap between the soft Bellman operator theory and standard Q-learning critic implementation deserves more explicit acknowledgment in the main text.

Detailed analysis of training compute overhead: Training requires drawing $K=100$ noise samples per batch item and evaluating both $Q$ and $\nabla_u Q$ to compute the importance weights and Stein control variates. While Table 2 demonstrates competitive overall wall-clock training time (benefiting from fewer generation steps during policy rollouts), a finer-grained breakdown of actor update compute and memory cost versus critic updates would be beneficial.

strengths: Compelling theoretical unification: The paper establishes an elegant and rigorous connection between two previously disjoint lines of research on diffusion policies targeting Boltzmann distributions—the noise-expectation family (e.g., QNE, SDAC) and the gradient-expectation family (e.g., iDEM, DQS)—showing they correspond to specific choices (isotropic control variate weight eta=0 and eta=1) within a general Langevin Stein posterior mean estimation framework.

Principled variance reduction via Langevin Stein control variates: The derivation of the generalized (matrix-valued) Langevin Stein operator and the closed-form coordinate-wise variance-minimizing coefficients (Lambda*) provides an effective way to combine zeroth-order Q-values and first-order Q-gradients, addressing the severe estimation variance inherent in self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS).

Principled extension to flow policies: By formulating the objective via reverse flow matching (regressing onto the posterior mean of the velocity), the work bypasses the need for target data samples or unstable backpropagation through ODE integration steps, extending Boltzmann policy matching beyond diffusion models to continuous-time flow matching.

Principled action boundary handling: The framework maps actions through an unconstrained latent space via tanh and incorporates the exact change-of-variables log-determinant (sech^2 Jacobian factor) into the unnormalized target, avoiding heuristic truncation methods that violate boundary probability flow.

Solid empirical evaluation: Validations on both a 2D multimodal target and 8 continuous-control tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite show consistent performance gains, lower sample variance across random seeds, and faster training/inference (10 ODE integration steps vs. 20–100 diffusion steps). Ablations in the appendix thoroughly isolate the impact of the learned control variates, proposal distributions, and the latent transformation.
weaknesses: Inference relies on test-time candidate filtering: During inference, the policy generates M=32 candidates and executes the one with the maximum Q-value. While this follows prior diffusion RL literature (e.g., MaxEntDP, QVPO), it convolves the quality of the learned flow distribution with test-time search/filtering. Reporting performance for pure single-sample execution (M=1) across all benchmark tasks would clarify how well the flow model alone has internalized the Boltzmann distribution.

Benchmark scope restricted to DMControl: Evaluation is conducted on standard DeepMind Control Suite environments (state/action dimensions up to ~20). Demonstrating performance on higher-dimensional or more complex contact-rich systems (e.g., Humanoid, Dexterous hand manipulation, or Isaac Gym environments) would further reinforce the scalability of the flow policy formulation.

Proposal distribution coverage in high dimensions: Theorem 4.2 relies on the mutual absolute continuity of the proposal distribution and true marginals. While this holds theoretically on R^d with Gaussian proposals, in high-dimensional action spaces SNIS proposal mismatch can cause effective sample sizes to drop significantly unless K is scaled up.
